readerTitle: Tupperware's parties: the growth engine that ran on customers' lives
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Tupperware, 1950년대 홈 파티 판매와 이후 쇠퇴) + 가상 적용 (사진 편집 앱)
insight: 성장 루프는 제품이 아니라 고객의 생활 방식 위에서 돈다. 그 생활이 바뀌면 제품이 좋아도 루프는 멈춘다.
misconception: 한 번 잘 돌던 성장 엔진은 제품만 좋으면 계속 돈다.

sources.text: PBS American Experience, "Tupperware!" (2004): 매장 판매 부진, 1951년 매장 철수와 홈 파티 전환, Brownie Wise의 역할
Bob Kealing, Tupperware Unsealed: Brownie Wise, Earl Tupper, and the Home Party Pioneers (University Press of Florida, 2008)
Smithsonian National Museum of American History, Tupperware 관련 소장품 및 설명 자료
Tupperware Brands, Chapter 11 신청 보도자료 (2024년 9월) 및 주요 언론 보도
Target 매장 판매 제휴(2000년대 초)와 종료에 관한 언론 보도

factChecks.note: Tupperware의 매장 철수 시점(1951년)과 Brownie Wise의 영업 총괄 임명 시점은 PBS American Experience와 Kealing(2008)으로 확인하세요.
Brownie Wise가 Detroit 인근(Dearborn, Michigan) 출신 홈 파티 판매자였다는 내용을 확인하세요. 카드에는 "Detroit-area"로만 적었습니다.
Target 제휴(2000년대 초 시작, 몇 년 안에 종료)와 그 기간 파티 판매 감소의 인과 관계는 보도마다 표현이 다릅니다. 카드에는 "reportedly"로 적었습니다. 시작·종료 연도를 확인하세요.
후반기 매출이 해외 시장 비중에 크게 의존했다는 서술을 연차보고서나 언론 보도로 확인하세요. 구체적 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
2024년 9월 미국 Chapter 11 신청을 확인하세요. 쇠퇴 원인(저가 경쟁 제품, 재무 문제)은 카드 7에 일반적으로만 적었습니다.
1970년대 이후 미국 여성의 경제활동 참가율 상승은 널리 기록된 사실입니다. 이것이 파티 판매 둔화의 한 원인이라는 해석은 여러 자료에 나오지만 단일 원인으로 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The container that wouldn't sell in stores
body: In the late 1940s, Earl Tupper's plastic containers sat on store shelves and barely moved. Shoppers didn't understand the airtight lid, and no one was there to show them.
A few years later, the same product was selling fast in living rooms across the US. The way it got there made the company famous. Later, it left the company exposed.

image.label: Plastic containers gathering dust on a store shelf
image.brief: 1940년대 후반 잡화점 선반. 파스텔색 플라스틱 밀폐 용기들이 먼지를 뒤집어쓴 채 쌓여 있고, 지나가는 손님은 관심 없이 지나침. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Stores or living rooms?
body: It's 1951. You make Tupperware. In stores it sells slowly. But a few independent dealers who sell at home parties, where they show how the seal works, are selling far more.

options.text: Keep stores and add home parties alongside them
options.feedback: You keep wide reach and spread your risk. But dealers may resent competing with a shelf down the street, and customers can skip the party.

options.text: Pull out of stores and sell only through home parties
options.feedback: Dealers get a reason to invest everything, and every sale comes with a demonstration. But all your growth now rides on one channel.

options.text: Stay in stores and pay for in-store demonstrations
options.feedback: You keep control and reach. But a stranger in an aisle earns less trust than a friend in her kitchen, and you pay for every demo.

choice.afterReveal: Each path trades reach against a sales engine that explains the product. Tupper chose B.

cards.title: Tupper bet everything on the party.
body: Tupper pulled Tupperware from stores in 1951. He put Brownie Wise, a Detroit-area saleswoman and one of the strongest party sellers, in charge of sales.
At a party, a dealer showed how the lid sealed with a soft "burp". Guests tried it, bought, and were asked to host a party of their own. Some hosts went on to become dealers.
Through the 1950s, sales grew quickly, and Wise became one of the best-known businesswomen in America.

cards.title: A loop, not a funnel
body: A **funnel** pours attention in at the top and keeps whoever comes out the bottom. A **growth loop** is different: each round of customers produces the next round.
list: A party sells to the guests
One guest agrees to host her own party
Her party brings in new guests
A few guests become dealers who run more parties
cards.callout: Every party planted the next one. The sales force recruited its own customers and its own replacements.
cards.softwareNote: The same shape appears when every shared file, invite or exported image brings in a new user, who then shares again.

cards.title: The loop ran on things outside the factory.
list: **A product that needed a demo:** the seal made sense once you saw it
**Trust:** buying from a friend felt safer than buying from an ad
**A way of life:** many suburban women were home in the daytime, had friends nearby, and welcomed a social afternoon and extra income
cards.callout: Only the first one was about the containers. The rest was about the customers' lives.
cards.softwareNote: A loop of shared links runs on where your users spend time online and what they like to share there.

cards.title: Then the fuel ran low.
body: From the 1970s on, many more American women worked outside the home. Fewer had free afternoons or neighbors at home to invite. The US loop slowed, even though the plastic was as good as ever. Growth leaned more on markets abroad, where parties still fit daily life.

Tupperware tried stores again. In the early 2000s it sold through Target, but party sales reportedly fell and the deal ended within a few years. In 2024, the company filed for bankruptcy protection in the US.

image.label: A circular arrow loop slowing down as a clock fills the center
image.brief: 원형 화살표 루프 인포그래픽: "Party → New host → New guests → New dealer". 루프 가운데에 출근 가방과 시계가 놓이고, 화살표 선이 점점 흐려지며 끊어지는 모습. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Don't blame one thing.
body: A slowing loop is only part of the story. Cheap containers filled supermarket shelves, and the company had financial trouble late in its life.

The lesson is narrower. A loop that runs on customers' habits can't be saved by improving the product. When the setting changes, you need a **new loop**, not a better lid. And selling in two channels at once can weaken the one your loop depends on.

cards.title: Now it's a photo app.
body: Your photo-editing app grew for years in one way. Users posted edited photos on one social network with a small "Edited with" tag, and friends tapped it to download.
That network changed how links appear, and fewer of your users post there now. New sign-ups are falling. What do you do?

options.text: Buy ads to replace the lost sign-ups
options.feedback: It stops the bleeding, but you've swapped a loop that fed itself for a funnel you pay to fill every month.

options.text: Find where users share now and rebuild the loop there
options.feedback: You follow the habit, not the old channel. It takes work and testing, but it can bring back growth that pays for itself.

options.text: Keep the tag as is. It worked for years
options.feedback: It costs nothing today, but the loop's fuel was user behavior, and that behavior has moved.

cards.title: A growth loop runs on your customers' lives.
body: Tupperware's parties worked because they fit how customers lived. When that changed, the loop slowed, no matter how good the product was.
**Try it today:** write down how your last ten customers found you. For each path, note one habit of theirs it depends on. Which habit is changing?
